issues.legal_issue: An emergency acquisition may proceed without a development scheme, and the government is not required to prepare one after taking possession.
material_facts: The government declared the land needed for a public purpose after determining that preparation of a development scheme was likely to be delayed.
The declaration was made without a development scheme having been prepared or sanctioned.
The government took possession and began putting the land to use, and the High Court ordered it to prepare a development scheme.
issues.conclusion: The emergency provision dispensed with the statutory requirement to prepare a development scheme, so the government was not bound to prepare one after taking possession and the mandamus was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5, 6, and 7 of the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, provide for acquisition after a sanctioned scheme and, separately, for an urgent acquisition without a scheme where the government is satisfied that preparation of a scheme is likely to be delayed. Section 7 dispenses with the scheme requirement rather than postponing it until after possession. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.emergency_land_acquisition: The proceeding is an emergency land acquisition.
predicates.government_found_scheme_preparation_like: The government determined that preparing a development scheme was likely to be delayed.
predicates.acquisition_declaration_made_without_sch: The government made the acquisition declaration before any development scheme had been prepared or sanctioned.

issues.definition: When an emergency land acquisition proceeds on the government's determination that preparing a scheme is likely to be delayed, and the acquisition declaration is made without a scheme, no scheme is required after possession.

issues.legal_issue: The distinction between acquisitions made under a development scheme and urgent acquisitions made without one does not constitute unconstitutional discrimination.
material_facts: The challenged law provided for acquisitions following preparation and sanction of a development scheme, as well as urgent acquisitions made without one.
The urgent procedure was intended to serve the law's public purposes, including settling immigrants who had been compelled to leave their homes.
The respondent argued that applying the urgent procedure to the acquisition discriminated against him.
issues.conclusion: The two classes of acquisition were identifiable and rationally related to the law's purpose, so the urgent-acquisition provision did not involve discrimination.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 of the Constitution permits a classification that distinguishes identifiable classes on a rational basis related to the purpose of the law. The Court found the distinction between scheme-based and urgent acquisitions rational in light of the Act's public purposes. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.equal_protection_challenge_to_emergency_: A person challenged an emergency land acquisition as unequal treatment.
predicates.acquisition_procedures_form_identifiable: The law provides distinct, identifiable procedures for acquisitions with a scheme and urgent acquisitions without one.
predicates.classification_rationally_related_to_pub: The distinction between the procedures is rationally related to the public purposes the law serves.

issues.definition: An equal-protection challenge to an emergency acquisition fails where the acquisition procedures form identifiable classes and the distinction is rationally related to a public purpose.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge under the fundamental-rights guarantees concerning property cannot invalidate a law protected by the constitutional provision shielding laws listed in the Ninth Schedule.
material_facts: The respondent challenged the acquisition law under the constitutional guarantees concerning property.
The challenged Act was listed in the Ninth Schedule.
The Court relied on the constitutional protection for listed laws rather than deciding the substantive merits of the asserted property-rights violations.
issues.conclusion: The challenge under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31(2) was futile because Article 31B protected the Act as a law listed in the Ninth Schedule.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B provides that Acts and provisions specified in the Ninth Schedule are not void on the ground that they are inconsistent with or abridge rights in Part III of the Constitution. The challenged Act was listed in the Ninth Schedule. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.fundamental_rights_challenge_to_acquisit: A person challenges an acquisition law on the ground that it violates a fundamental right.
predicates.challenged_law_listed_in_protected_sched: The challenged law is listed in a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from invalidation on fundamental-rights grounds.

issues.definition: A fundamental-rights challenge cannot invalidate an acquisition law when that law is listed in a constitutionally protected schedule.
